A STUDENT MURDERER.

TIEPIN, O., November 5.—The preliminary trial of Charles Madder, a student, who murdered Miss Phoebe Bernard on Thursday night, because she declined to marry him, is in progress. A great deal of excitement is manifested, and fears are entertained that if the result of the trial is not satisfactory, Madder will be lynched.

KICKED TO DEATH.

AUGUSTA, Ga., November 5.—Last night two colored men named James Barnett and Moses Martin had a difficulty. They engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle and Martin kicked Burnett to death.

NOT GUILTY.

NAPOLEON, Ohio, November 6.—At 11 a. m. the jury in the Gev. Scott murder case returned a verdict of not guilty.

A MULE THIEF KILLED.

CINCINNATI, November 6.—Little Rock special says that Deputy Sheriff McDonald shot and killed Felix Burell, a mule thief, during a running fight in Monroe county yesterday and McDonald was badly wounded. Burell stole a mule from a widow two months ago and yesterday came back and stole another.

TRAN MEN INDICTED.

SANFORD, Ky, November 6.—L. F. McNama, conductor, and Wm Taite, engineer of the train, that killed five men at McKinney, on the Cincinnati Southern Railway two weeks ago, have been indicted for murder in the first degree. They ran off immediately after the collision and have not since been heard of. The Governor will offer a reward for their capture.

SENTENCED TO BE HUNG.

JERSEY CITY, N. J., November 6.—Kanskowski, who murdered Mina Muller, was to-day sentenced to be hanged on January 6th, 1882. When asked if he had anything to say why sentence of death should not be pro-
changed on January 6th, 1882. When asked if he had anything to say why sentence of death should not be pronounced upon him he said "God knows that since this court house was built no more innocent man has been within it, God knows this." ROW AT A DANCE.

ATLANTA, Ga., November 6.—Several white men went to a negro dance near Carmad last night and got into drunken row with some negroes. Elias Edwards (white) was shot in the temple by Austin Howard, a negro, and killed. Another white man was not though not fatally. The negro escaped.

HER ASSAILANT A NEGRO—EXCITEMENT AT ROCK-VILLE, MD.—THREATS OF LYNCHING.

Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR.

Rockville, Md., November 21.—This community was shocked on Saturday evening last by nearing of the brutal and indecent assault committed on a five year old daughter of Charles Lochte, a store-keeper at Montrose, a settlement about four miles from here, on the turnpike leading to Washington, by a negro farm hand named Charles Rigney. The fiend got the little girl to go to the barn with him to look up something which he said he had lost. Mr. Lochte was busy at the store at the time, and his first intimation as to the terrible crime that had been committed was in seeing the girl come from the barn, her clothes being literally torn from her. After learning the facts, Mr. Lochte started after the negro. His tracks were found, showing that he had gone into the woods. In a little while he was overtaken and would have been killed on the spot by the enraged father of the child, but he was prevented from doing so by those who had assisted him in the capture. With four other men Mr. Lochte tied and bound the negro securely with a rope, and placing him in a wagon drove him to this place, when he was regularly surrendered to Sheriff Kelchener and by him turned over to Jailor Kingsbury. On the way up from Montrose one of the five tied a rope around the neck of the prisoner. It was with this rope that he was led after he was lifted out of the wagon. It is said that the lynching would have taken place before the jail was reached had not two of the five men indulged a little too freely in cider just before they started from Montrose.

Rigney made a similar attempt on a little girl about a year ago. He left the neighborhood in consequence of it and only recently returned. Prior to that it is charged that he endeavored to get another girl to go into the woods with him. He was seen in jail by THE STAR correspondent this morning. He was hideous enough before, no doubt, but now has a bruised eye and swollen nose, the result of the pounding that Mr. Lochte gave him when he caught him. He denies the crime, but his denial is not given any consideration, for he was seen going to the barn with the child and then caught as he was running away. He said he thought some people would have come to hang him last night, and was extremely glad that no such visit was made him.

There were threats of lynching him heard on Saturday night and again yesterday, but better counsel prevailed until the grand jury has heard the evidence. The grand jury met this morning and is now in session. Several witnesses have been examined. Should they find an indictment for rape, the impression is that the ravisher will be taken out of jail to-night and lynched on the same tree that Diggs, the colored ravisher, was hanged about a year ago. This will save the state expense, as the law hangs all convicted for rape. Should the indictment be for an attempt at rape, he will not be lynched, but he will undoubtedly get the full extent of the law in the penitentiary ten years. It therefore depends entirely on the action of the grand jury whether or not Rigney will see another morning's sunrise. Report comes here that a party is being organized at Montrose to come here to-night. Several have received invitations to "meet at Rockville, on important business." Sheriff Kelchener says he fully expected an attack on the jail last night, but does not apprehend any for to-night, as he thinks the excitement has quieted down. The jailor, to be on the safe side, has taken extra precautions to keep his prisoner. Rigney says he is but nineteen years of age. He looks at least four years older. M. J.

A Revolting Assault Upon a Child.
ROCKVILLE, MD., Nov. 20.—The five year old daughter of Charles Loehle, who resides at Montrose, in Montgomery county, was brutally and indecently assaulted by a colored man named Charles Rigney, who worked on an adjoining farm, on Saturday afternoon. The negro enticed the girl into a stable; the act was discovered soon afterwards and the negro arrested by the girl's father, who would have killed him on the spot had it not been for the interference of others, who assisted in bringing him to the jail here.

There was talk of lynching him last night, and the talk was resumed tonight, but so far nothing have been done in that direction. The grand jury will be in session tomorrow, and the evidence will be heard.
charles-rigney-rockville-1881-11-19.A7: THE MONTROSE, M.D., OUTRAGE CASE.—A special to the Baltimore Sun from Rockville, Md., November 25, says: The grand jury here to-day returned an indictment against Rigney, charging him with an attempt at outrage. His victim is not injured so much as was at first thought, and the chances of his lynching have about passed away. Still there is a feeling that he should suffer the severest penalty, his intent having been as guilty as if he had succeeded in the consummation of his heinous purpose. Had the indictment been for the extreme offence he would certainly have been lynched. Under the circumstances it is thought the law will be allowed to take its course.

A Brutal Outrage.—It appears that the terrible and swift vengeance which was broken upon the negro Diggs in this county a little over a year ago, has been forgotten or has lost its salutary effect upon a certain class of the colored population, for, on Saturday night our community was startled by a report that a similar crime had been committed at Montrose, a small, scattered village, about two miles from Rockville on the pike leading to Georgetown, but in the main is stripped of the horrid and repulsive features of the Diggs affair. In this instance a little five-year old daughter of Mr. Chas. Lochte being the victim, and Charles Rigney, a colored lad, the culprit.

On the afternoon of the day in question, Mrs. Lochte, while busily engaged in the domestic duties of her household, supposed their little daughter was in the store with its father, and he, that the child was with its mother, but in this they were both mistaken, for the negro had enticed her to the stable by offering her twenty-five cents to accompany him. The little victim was quite a favorite or pet with the frequenters at Mr. Lochte's store, and many a nickle and penny fell into her palm from admiring friends. In her childish and confiding simplicity it was no wonder she accompanied him and was by him brutally assaulted and outraged. The little child, as soon as it could escape the clutches of this fiend, went to the house, where the mother soon discovered the true state of affairs and informed her husband who called the negro out of his store and accused him of the crime, after which he proceeded to give him a severe thrashing, and possibly if some cooler heads had not been present, there would have been a darky funeral in that locality soon after; but the crowd interfered and saved the worthless life of the scoundrel. Rigney was then securely bound, placed in a wagon and brought before Justice Morgan, of this place, who, after hearing the evidence, committed him for the action of the grand jury then in session, who found a bill of attempted rape. In conversation with the physician who attended the little child, we learn that her injuries are not of a serious nature, but this does not lessen the enormity of the crime and the punishment it deserves. The intent of the villain cannot be doubted, and a sure and speedy punishment should follow. The security of female virtue demand it, the morals of every community claim this of the law, and every law-abiding citizen should see that it is enforced; and should moral suasion, law, conscience and common decency fail to prevent a repetition of this kind, there is for criminals of this character a terrible ultimatum held in reserve. There is a limit to all human endurance and patience, and when that point is passed in cases like the present a swift retribution follows the steps of crime.

This creature Rigney, says he is about nineteen years of age, and it is rumored that this is the second offence of this kind in which he was an active participant. If such should prove to be the case we think a jury could do no better service to the community and the culprit in particular than to send him to the penitentiary for a term of eight or ten years. "Out west," it is more than probable the local newspapers would briefly report this case in about the following language: "He was unanimously chosen by a convention of property holders to jump from the tail end of a wagon into the sweet subsequently."

THE FATE OF A MURDERER.
Tragic Death of the Texas usually Who Killed
Porter, the Actor.
PHILADELPHIA March 30 United
PHILADELPHIA, March 30. — United States Marshal Kerns received information this afternoon from Los Vegas, New Mexico, to the effect that James Currie, the murderer of Porter, the actor, was shot and killed at that place on March 24th. Currie, it appears, was on a drunken spree and threatened to kill several people. Among the persons threatened was a bartender of a saloon who, in self-defense, shot the Texan murderer. The ball entered his forehead and came out at the back of his head. A party of railroad hands, friends of the dead man, attempted to lynch the bartender, but the sheriff succeeded in getting him to jail. A coroner's inquest was held and the jury at once returned a verdict of shooting in self-defense. The assailant was held, as further trouble was expected.

THE BIG LAND SWINDLE.

St. Louis, March 30.—The United States grand jury is investigating the big land swindle recently discovered here. Cyrus Smith, real estate operator in Chicago, lately indicted for conspiring to defraud the government in presenting straw bonds from match factories, was brought here this morning from the Chicago jail by United States Marshal Gilman under a writ of habeas corpus, and will testify before the jury. It is said he has a large amount of information regarding the operations of the land ring. J. S. Wolfe, another real estate agent, of Chicago, was brought in on an attachment this morning, and will also be required to tell what he knows about the frauds.

MONTREAL, March 30.—The passenger and freight depots of the Occidental railway burned this forenoon. SUNDAY, APRIL 3, 1881.
THE doctrine of special Provi-
dence is denied by many, and belief of such is often branded as mere superstition, yet things will occur now and then which give a strong support to the beliefs in the special Providence theory. The New York Evening Post cites an event of this kind as occurring in New Mexico:

Two years ago, on March 20, at Marshal, in Texas, a well-known actor named Benjamin C. Porter was shot and killed by James C. Currie. It was generally held that the circumstances were peculiarly atrocious, and the evidence justified a condemnatory view that was accepted throughout the country. The trouble arose from some offensive remarks made by Currie about a lady and in her presence. Her companion, Mr. Porter and Mr. Barrymore, resisted this in no unbecoming fashion, and upon this slender provocation, Currie drew a revolver and shot Porter down.

The assassin was arrested, taken from the officers by a crowd of citizens who sought to lynch him, recaptured by the authorities, confined in prison and tried after a long delay for murder. His accuittal June last aroused wide indignation. But the proceeding was at all events legal, and Currie was released and disappeared. Just a week ago, on Thursday, March 24—almost exactly two years after the killing of Porter—Currie was shot dead in a bar-room at Les Vegas, in New Mexico, the ball entering his forehead and coming out at the back of his head. His slayer was a bartender whom Porter had previously threatened to shoot, but the menaced man was too quick for him.

History repeated itself in another way. Not only was this homicide, like the former one, committed in a drinking place, but there was an attempt to lynch the perpetrator and there was a rescue by the officers of the law. Nor does the parallel end here. For the coroner's inquest that was promptly held at Les Vegas resulted in an aquittal of Currie's assailant on the ground of self-defense, and the man has now been set free.

Civil Service Reformers. BOSTON, Nov. 10.—The secretary of the Cambridge Civil Service Reform Association has received a letter from the central committee of the National Civil Service Reform League informing him of a resolve by the committee to send a delegation to wait upon President Arthur soon after the assembling of Congress in regular session, inviting the Cambridge Association to add one more delegate. The central committee of the League, as now constituted, will be the nucleus of the deputation which will be increased, it is expected, by delegates from many of the important civil service associations throughout the country. The movement is designed not only to represent to the President the views of the associations regarding civil service, but particularly to impress the public with the nature and importance of this reform. A Liberal Spaniard.
MADRID, Nov. 10.—In the Chamber of Deputies to-day, r Senor Moel declared himself a partisan of the constitution of 1869, as it was capable of securing the enjoyment of the rights of individuals under the popular monarchy of King Alfonso, and because it harmonized with the wishes of the people. Senor Morel urged the introduction of jury and magisterial system, similar to those in England and America, and laws insuring respect for property, similar to those in Belgium and England. OWINGSVILLE, Nov. 10.—William Royce, who has been intimate with a young woman named Jennie Burke, in Fleming County, for over two years, went over to see her and found a young man named Jacob Rogers visiting her. A report has just reached here that Royce died last night.

joe-harris-marble-hall.A1:
THAT DOUBLE MURDER.
Speedy Arrest of the Bloody- Handed Villain.
The Booty Found on Him---Anticipations of Lynch Law.
Further Details of the Horrible and Blood Curdling Affair.
at Marble Hall, Hawkins county, near Rogersville, Monday night, in which Charles Brown and Andy Heck were brutally killed, as was stated in our columns, divided the honors yesterday with the Roane county poisoning horror in the way of sensation in local circles, and the two set everybody on the qui vive to learn the latest news.

The noon train yesterday brought the news in a note to the CHRONICLE from our Rogersville correspondent of the capture of the perpetrator of the dastardly deed—a man by the name of Harris. The capture was effected at midnight Tuesday night, and the prisoner was taken to Rogersville and jailed. The pocket-book taken from Brown, together with the money stolen, one of our informants says $255 and a bank check for $40, made payable to Mr. Brown, this being the result of his sale of hogs at Whitesburg the day before his murder.

We were unable to learn the first name of Harris, but understand that he lives in Hancock county. There are two brothers of them, desperate men. He was captured while making his way out of the county. As we are informed Harris put up a story, when a rope was put around his neck, that he was not the man who committed the murder, that another man—he did not say who—did the deed, took the money, handed it to him (Harris) on the outside of the door and then got out of the way. This story is not credited, however, and all the indications pointed to Harris as the only participant in the most foul and bloody manner which has stained the annals of East Tennessee history for years.

It is said that the whole country around was terribly stirred up and aroused over the matter, as is perfectly natural, and the indignation had reached such a pitch that it was anticipated that short work would be made of the hardened wretch last night, and that the courts would never be bothered with him. An effort was made by us to obtain late information last night, but the absence of telegraphic communication and inconvenience of railroad connection prevented it.

The Rogersville papers, which came by mail yesterday, give additional details of the terrible affair which so shocked the community. According to the account of the Spectator, Mr. Wm. Price, who lives across the road from Marble Hall, spent the evening till bedtime with Messrs. Brown & Heck, who were remaining that night there preparatory to leaving for Bristol the next day. The property had been sold by Mr. Brown's father to a Mr. Blackley, of Virginia, and his wife was there in another room of the same house, which is a very large one. Mrs. Price was sleeping with Mrs. Blackley. Mr. Price was up about 1 o'clock in the night and discovered a light in the room occupied by Brown and Heck. He went over and aroused his wife and on entering the room occupied by Brown and Heck made the ghastly discovery of their murder, and found the feather bed on fire. Had the discovery not have been made at the time, the building would no doubt have burned. Thus it is that the villain set fire to the house hoping by this means to cover up the murder.

It seems that the deadly work was done with the pole of an ax, both the victims having their skulls crushed. The assassin must certainly have been very skillful and effective to escape without arousing others in the house.

The Press and Times says Brown had $210 dollars in money and a check for $40. Brown was a man between 25 and 30 years of age, a son-in-law of Henderson Fudge, of Doughertyville, and leaves a wife and two children, who were in Bristol, as has been stated by us. Heck was a youth of 17, son of Fayette Heck, who lived with Brown.

The News says Mr. Brown has two brothers in Bristol, Alex. and John, the former being a twin brother of the unfortunate man. All the brothers were about to engage in the carriage building business in Bristol. His brothers said he had a few bitter enemies and they were unable to determine at first whether that or the greed for plunder was the object of the assassin. The two brothers and the wife and children left Bristol for the awful scene Tuesday.

THE ROGERSVILLE MURDER.
How the Murderer was Caught----
No Lynching----All Quiet.
Our readers are conversant with the facts of the attrocious double murder of Chas. Brown and young Andy Heck, at Marble Hall, near Roger-ville, Monday night. As to the capture of Harris, the perpetrator, the following letter gives further particulars:

BULL'S GAP, Nov. 24, 1880.

MR. EDITOR: Yesterday, while the inquest was being held over the bodies of Brown and Heck, there was a man present by the name of Harris who seemed to be very restless and started off. The sheriff got some one to ask him where he was going. He said he was going to a grocery near there, and started off. The sheriff seeing that he did not go to the grocery, followed him about three miles and arrested him and placed him under guard.

Harris had a brother who assisted Brown in getting some hogs to Whitesburg the day before that he had sold, and he was missing. The sheriff and one of his deputies started to Hancock county, where the Harrises come from, thinking they would find him there, and on their road they heard of him passing at the foot of Clinch mountain about daylight. They followed him and captured him that evening or night and lodged him in jail at Rogersville this morning before daylight. He had about $200 that he said he took from Brown after he was killed. He said he got a check and hid it under a fence corner. He said he did not do the killing; he said it was a ruffian, but would not tell his name. The supposition is that the two brothers did the killing, and the first one that was arrested had started to tell the other how every thing was. After they had murdered the men they set the bed on fire, and would have burned the house down had it not been for a Mr. Price living within a few yards of the house. He smelt the feathers burning, examined his house, but could not find anything on fire, and went over to the house where the murder was committed and asked the lady of the house what that was. She said she did not know, and told him to go in the boys' room, maybe it was something in there. As he opened the door the room was so full of smoke he could not see anything. He went to the bed to wake them, put his hand on Brown's head and found it was mashed up. He then raised the alarm that they were murdered, got them off the bed and threw the portion of the bed that was not burned out in the yard. There were two white ladies in the house. If they had waked while the murderers were in the house they would have probably been treated likewise. J. J. K.

From Mr. H. M. Aiken, who returned from Rogersville on yesterday's noon train, we learn that everything is now quiet, and Harris is in jail. There was a strong feeling and suspicions of lynching Wednesday night, but the sheriff succeeded in quelling the spirit and persuading the indignant crowd to let the law take its course.

But in the middle of that large cell there is an iron cage ten feet square and six or seven feet high. It is made of huge bars of iron, bolted and securely riveted at each crossing of the bars, which are not more than four inches apart. On its doors of similar structure are three huge patent pad locks. His feet are secured by heavy felters, and to these is secured a strong chain which passes between the bars and is anchored on the outside. Over this grim grip of doom presides Jailor Cook, a man who picks up his Navy six shooter when he goes to let you peep through those bars, and who will just die there before his game can get away. The people are now quiet, but Joe Harris will surely have to face his jury. Capt. Cook opened the door, a work of several minutes, and at a word Harris bounded with his chain to the door, looked us squarely in the face (Walker of the Spectator, and Dungan of the Jonesboro Journal were with me) jerked off his hats, and said, "Well here I am gentlemen, what do you think of me?" I was prepared to see a fiend. I thought God had set his mark on a man, who at midnight could coldly and dexterously brain two men and fire a house containing sleeping women and children for the purpose of robbing one of them to get his purse with the price of a few hogs in it. But I was greatly surprised. He was bright and good looking, 5 feet 8 inches high, weighing about 140 to 150, aged 25. His skin was fair, eye clear and, save a light moustache of red color, and a very short glossy beard that served to lie back on his chin, he seemed either cleanly shaven or youthfully beardless. His head was well enough shaped and, though he said he could neither read nor write, he had readiness and accuracy of speech and an intelligent appearance. He told the same old story, with which he whiled away the dark hour in which Blevins brought him across Clinch Mountain.

During the day however he acknowledged from his cage to Blevins that he had lied to him. He shed tears, said he knew he had to die and meant thereafter to lie to him no more. From what I could see of him he is lithe and agile as a fox, as active as a hare, and I thought that under the silken beard, fair skin, clear eye and handsome hair I could catch feeble gillipses of the devil in him. I believe he killed those men, but I don't believe he was alone in it. The people of Rogersville believe he is the sole murderer, and Sheriff Blevins, who has certainly distinguished himself as a detective of rare sackidity hind nerve, agrees with them in that opinion. He thinks all of Brown's money is accounted for except the bag of silver, and that he may have disposed of that in several ways. His opinion is entitled to great weight. If it be established that he had all the money Blevins' theory will be conclusively proven. I know he may have killed both. I think he did. But there are so many probabilities that a man would foresee, not only possible failure in a double murder unadded, but absolute detection to follow, that I doubt, if he would have been bold enough to unpertake it without having a confederate standing near to make failure impossible. Extorting a Confession—Torturing a Murderer to an Acknowledgement of Crime.

BRISTOL, Jan. 23.—The trial of Joe Harris, the alleged Marble Hall murderer, is set for Monday, at Rogersville, before Judge Hacker, but he has not yet succeeded in obtaining counsel, while numbers have volunteered to prosecute him. The stories of his legs bursting from frost-bite during the recent cold weather are probably untrue, but that he has had to submit to torture since his first imprisonment cannot be doubted. Several attempts have been made, with only partial success, to extort from him such confession as would lead to the discovery of more evidence against him. On one occasion he was hanged and the rope broke, letting him fall. After regaining consciousness he admitted that he had lied, and proposed to tell the truth and show where he had deposited the papers from Brown's pocketbook. He said the implement with which he had killed Brown and Ack would be found in the cistern, and that he was concealed in the house

when it was closed at bedtime, and that he had waited on a neighboring hill to witness the burning of the house. The papers were not found at the point he indicated. Little confidence is placed in any of his statements. I am not able to say how much further his torture has been proceeded with, and it is doubtful if a jury can be obtained in Hawkins to try him.

The conviction as to his guilt may be said to be unanimous and the feeling against him is very great. No doubt is entertained that he will be hung for the coldest double murder and attempted eremation ever known in East Tennessee. Since his first torture it has transpired that contrary to his protestations he had taken the overcoat and pocket knife of one of his victims to Pumpkin Valley and left them with his mother, where they were found. There is no public censure of those who have tortured him, for such is the feeling over the murder at midnight of all the males in the house and his attempt not only to burn their bodies, but to destroy by fire the lives of two lonely ladies who were sleeping in the large mansion, and his confessed cool, deliberate perch on the wooden hill to witness the work of the flames. that his lynching would be witnessed without a shudder by the public.

TO SWING.
Joe Harris Guilty of Murder in the First Degree.
The Voice of Brown's and Heck's Blood Crying from the Ground.
The jury last Thursday, after sitting five days at Rogerville, brought in a verdict of guilty of murder in the first degree, against Joe Harris, for the murder of Brown and Heck on the night of Nov. 22nd, 1880. Harris was assigned able counsel, who did for him all that his bad case admitted of. The pocket-book, money, blood, pocket-koife, overcoat, the presence at Marble Hall, the flight to Pumpkin Valley, could not be satisfactorily explained, save on the supposition that Joe Harris had done the murder, which his knowledge of the men and premises, made so easy for him to do. He made no confession, but went through the blood curdling ordeal unmoved, as he must have gone through the bloody scenes of that awful night of November. At the reading of the verdict it is said he smiled. Doubtless he smiled as the skulls of poor Brown and Heck crushed beneath his murderous blows. Part of his scheme was foiled when Price found the house on fire in time to save it and the dead bodies and the helpless ladies and children who were sleeping within it. Another and perhaps dearer feature of his scheme failed, when the fleet-footed, intrepid and sagacious Bob Blevins overtook him and folded his design to use and enjoy Brown's hard earned money, and after a few brief and terrible months he will witness the speedy failure of his purpose to live on in heartless triumph as the Champion flend of Hawkins county. The people have decided he shall surrender his life in a manner that will terrify evil doers for many a day to come. At the earnest request of Harris his counsel appealed to the Supreme Court which will afford delay in the final decision. The court will consider the evidence and the facts before making a final decision.

THE DEATH SENTENCE.
Joe Harris, the Marble Hall Murderer, to Hang November 25th

The Supreme Court yesterday, in a learned, elaborate and impressive opinion delivered by Judge Freeman, affirmed the decision of the court below in the case of Joe Harris, the Marble Hall murderer, and sentenced the prisoner to hang, within legal hours and distance from the court-house at Rogersville, Friday, November 25th.

Harris committed the double murder of Charley Brown and Andy Heck in the famous Marble Hall property near Rogersville, on the night of November 23, 1880, the horrible details of the crime being, yet fresh in the minds of all. He was tried at Rogersville, convicted and sentenced by Judge N. Hacker to hang April 1, 1881, but appealed. Now he will be executed just one year, lacking two days, after the commission of the crime. The prisoner will be taken back to the Rogersville jail and kept securely confined until the date of the hanging.

Henry Johnston, Colored, Hanged for Murder at Sumter, S. C.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Sumter, S. C., Nov. 25.—Henry Johnston, a colored man, was hanged here today for the murder of John Davis, also colored, on the 5th of last February.

Executions in South Carolina are now conducted in private, and the throng of gaping and excited negroes who usually attend on such occasions has been stricken out from the incidents of a modern hanging. The change is a decided improvement, as it deprives the event of that theatrical character which is so injurious to the common mind, and which frequently converted the convict into a hero and a martyr. In keeping with the new regulations there were present at the execution of Henry Johnston only the following persons: The Sheriff and his deputies, a detail of men from the Sumter Light Infantry, armed, but in plain clothes, members of the press, clergymen, physicians, and a few citizens designated by the Sheriff—in all about fifty persons. A considerable number were in the street adjoining the jail-yard, and got occasional glimpses of the execution. Henry Johnston, the convicted murderer, is a tall and rather spare man, a dark mulatto, or what is called a "mustee." His face does not indicate a natural tendency to crime. His appearance, on the whole, is rather gentle. He had passed his time quietly for the few days preceding his execution. He had become a Roman Catholic, and was frequently visited by the Sisters of Mercy, who have an establishment and school in this place. A few days ago he requested the Sheriff to give him AN EXTRA GOOD BREAKFAST on the morning of his execution, and expressed the desire for a biscuit to be given him when he should ascend the scaffold, showing that he had not forgotten his bodily comfort while preparing his soul for the inevitable death which awaited him. He has frequently expressed the opinion that Orange Isaac, the dealer in charms, ought to suffer death with him. It is also said that he confidently looked for a reprieve from the Governor. The weather, which had been extremely gloomy for several days, grew colder and clearer yesterday. Today it is very cold, with ice on the ground for the first time this season. The convict, however, passed a comfortable night, and rested well, in spite of the cold weather. The scaffold was a primitive structure, built of plue scantling, two upright posts, with a piece mortised in at the top. At a convenient height from the ground two plank shelves, supported by heavy plate hinges, not in the centre. These were propped up from below and approached by a rough flight of steps. The prisoner stood upon this, and the rope was secured to the beam above. The supports being knocked from under the shelves they would fall, and the drop would hang the culprit. Before the hour for the execution I was informed that a bountiful breakfast was provided for Johnston, of which he ate heartily. Yesterday he regaled himself with sweet elder and crackers as an extra lunch.

THE AUTHORITIES BEEMING ANXIOUS to indulge him in any manner consistent with their duty. It was the intention of the Sheriff to have had the hanging as early as possible during the prescribed hours, but the sudden death of a colored man had rendered the summoning of a Coroner's jury necessary, and the living had to await on the dead. Meantime the scaffold had been raised in the jallyard, midway between the barn and the western fence of the yard, and everything was got ready for the execution. At a little after 12 o'clock the Sheriff and the persons permitted to attend the execution left the Sheriff's office in a body. Arriving at the jail, they found the premises strongly guarded, and only those were admitted who were on a list furnished to the gate-keepers. Soon after our arrival

THE PRISONER was brought down from his cell, his hands secured behind him by handcuffs. He looked calm, though rather pale, and walked with a firm step. He was accompanied by Father McNeill, of the Catholic Church, and the Rev. J. B. Middleton, colored, and a pretty strong guard. On reaching the scaffold, Father McNeill addressed the prisoner in an undertone, to which he assented, and repeated some words after the priest. The Deputy Sheriff then read the sentence of the Court by which Johnson was tried. After this the priest again addressed the prisoner. Johnson was dressed in dark tweed pants, a white shirt without collar, and a black frock coat, buttoned. At twenty minutes past 13 he ascended the fatal steps and whispered a few words to the Sheriff, asking him not to permit his body to fall when it was cut down after execution, and requested him not to forget to send certain letters which the prisoner had written to friends in another county. The ropo was then adjusted around his neck, and his arms were plianced together. His legs were also tied together. A black cap was drawn over his head and face, completely concealing his features. The Sheriff and his Deputy then took leave of him. The Sheriff then, standing at the foot of the steps, said: "Johnson, are you ready?" and he replied "Yes," in a calm but rather weak voice. Then, at twenty-five minutes past 13, the prop which supported the platform was pulled from under it, and

without any perceptible sound. It first hung very quietly, but soon began to jerk and struggle with hands and feet, which was continued for a few minutes. When these movements ceased the doctors, Mood and Boyd, ascended the steps and examined the body, but found that the heart was still beating. The body was allowed to remain hanging eight minutes longer, when, upon a second examination, the doctors pronounced life extinct. The body was then carefully cut down. The doctors again examined it and found the neck completely broken. This was a great relief to the bystanders, who had

was delivered to Father McNeill, who, in the absence of any friends or relatives, undertook to have it interred. Everything was conducted in a very quiet and orderly manner. It was Sheriff Durant's first public act since his appointment by the Governor to fill a vacancy caused by death, and he performed his painful and unpleasant duty with that quiet dignity which characterizes the good and upright man. There is very little feeling in the community on the subject of the execution. Everybody thinks the deceased prisoner guilty of the crime, and that he suffered justly the extreme penalty of the law.

A REMARKABLE CASE.

The case is one of the most remarkable recorded in the criminal annals of South Carolina. The details brought out during the trial read more like a romantic, weird narrative of the dark ages than the sober record of true events occurring in this enlightened nineteenth century. The case was tried before the celebrated Judge Thomas Jefferson Mackey, to whom your correspondent is indebted for the subjoined facts connected with the trial.

Both the prisoner and his victim were negroes, and the trial developed the system of voudoolsm or fetichism to which many of the negroes in South Carolina are still addicted. The prisoner before the trial made the following confession, which, after some lively sparring between the lawyers on both sides, was admitted as evidence: Johnston stated that he was desperately in love with the wife of the deceased—a woman about 25 years of age, the prisoner being near 50. That she repelled his advances and sought the aid of a conjurer, out Orange Isaacs, an aged

knew nothing about the latter, and would not say much of his mothea. I said no more to him and slept for an hour or so, until daylight, when the sheriff appeared and released me from my voluntary confinement.

Before 10 o'clock the streets were full of countrymen on horseback and afoot, and by 12 o'clock as many as 2000 or 2500 had gathered about the hotels, stores and the jail. A large police was around the jail and considerable excitement prevailed. A great many in the crowd were drinking freely and everybody was impatient for the ceremonies to begin.

About half past twelve a man named Wirt Gammon, who had put upon his coat without authority a police badge, attempted to disperse the crowd in front of the jail. He was drunk and rode his horse through the crowd and ordered everybody to move back. Sheriff Blevins took the badge away from him and jerked him off the horse. Gammon resisted and a struggled ensued.

THE GREATEST EXCITEMENT
prevailed. The crowd yelled and cheered Blevins, who drew his pistol and put Gammon under arrest, and several deputies took him into the jail and confined him. During the struggle Gammon was stripped of every rag from his waist up. During this excitement Harris was very nervous, believing that the crowd were attempting to capture and lynch him. The excitement soon subsided, and at fifteen minutes to one Harris was taken to the wagon, the rope, a three-quarter inch Manilla, nine feet in length, was put on his head, and sitting upon his coffin, he began his last ride.

The scene of the execution was reached in 20 minutes. The gallows, a rough affair, was in the same spot where Berry was hanged several years ago, and a large crowd had gathered in the hollow and around the hills. While the rope was being adjusted, Harris confessed his guilt in a very unintelligible and incoherent manner, repeating many of the words which will be found in his written confession elsewhere. He had been given several drinks of whisky while on the way to the gallows and was staggering drunk, and unable to articulate plainly. His harrange was tiresome, and amounted to nothing. It was a relief when his time was up and the horses were driven from under the doomed wretch and his body dropped to the rope's end. His neck was not broken; he was strangled to death, as was Webb in Knoxville. He made little or no struggle and in 22 minutes life was extinct. When the wagon was driven out Sheriff Blevins gave Harris a push, remarking, "If this isn't a gilt-edged affair you may have my hat!"

After the body had hung 35 minutes it was cut down and put into the coffin. The remins were taken in charge by a cousin of Harris named Robert Tate. What disposi-
was made of them we do not know.

An effort was made by one or two doctors of Rogersville to secure the body for dissection. Harris would not consent to have his body cut up, and it is probable that no effort will be made to violate his wish. The miserable carcass will mingle with earth, and Joe Harris will only be remembered because of the notoriety his heinous crimes gave him. Hawkins County is well rid of him, and it is questionable whether any other other locality has made a valuable acquisition.

WASHINGTON December 12, 1907

A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.

Specia Correspondence of the Register.

WASHINGTON, December 12.—I met Mr. J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette county, here to-day, and had considerable talk with him concerning the recent miners troubles in the Kanawha section. He is a middle aged, muscular and plucky looking individual, and seems like the right sort of a man to hold his own in a rough community. He said he thought the troubles in his section of the State had been settled for the time being, and had been settled in the only way in which it was possible to settle them. "It had come to be a mere question," he said, "whether the coal operators in the coal valley should control their own property or not; and as the miner's association was so constructed and extended that trespassers could not be punished under the present laws, the only way to get along was to meet

Force With Force

when trespasses were attempted. I advised Wyant, one of the larger operators in the valley, whose employees were about to be interfered with, that if he posted his place and warned the strikers not to come on it, that he would have the right to keep them off, and, if necessary, shoot and drag them off. "Well," said Wyant, "if that is the law, I'll keep 'em off," and getting a box of shotguns he put them in the hands of trusted employees, and has been free from annoyance ever since.

The Faulkners, who have mines in the same neighborhood, pursued the same course and with the same success, and Eugene Dana, who manages the Campbell's creek mines, a little lower down, get along comfortably by exhibiting similar nerve when threatened.

As to the Recent Trouble

at Strain's, he said, the strike was ostensibly made against the railroad in the first instance, the men admitting that the operators could not pay the advance asked without an increase in the price paid for coal by the C. & O. agency. The mine owners used every effort to get an advance, and when they were unsuccessful offered their former miners a chance to go back to work at the old prices before trying the experiment of importing colored miners. The old hands refused to take hold or allow any one else, and got the first set of negroes imported to stop, by threatening their lives if they did not, and offering to take care of them if they did. It was in this part of the transaction that the women figured, assembling at the pitmouth with pans and sticks, their husbands and friends meanwhile congregating in the vicinity to the

Number of Several Hundred.

"You may not think a demonstration by women would amount to much," added St. Clair, "but when you come to tackle a crowd of square-built English and Welsh women, some of whom can whip an ordinary man in a fist-fight without any trouble, it is not so trifling a thing." Anyhow it was enough, aided by the backing at hand, to scare out the new hands, and some of them craw'ed out through the air-course in preference to facing the mob. The next lot brought on were negroes of the same class, and it was a mere question of protecting or abandoning the owners in their right to work them. The strikers, numbering about 400, were waiting for the negroes at the station, and the county officials

Were Powerless

to assert their authority and protect the new hands. The Sheriff, Tyree, is a man of good courage and equal good sense. He knew he could get no pass sufficient to bear him out in the immediate neighborhood. He had the right to call on the nearest organized military company or battalion for assistance without consulting the Governor, but he thought the authority of the Chief Executive would have weight, and the Governor promptly gave him permission to use such authority for the purpose of doing what he had a right to do without it. That was all there was of it. We got two companies on the ground and guarded the negroes from intrusion a couple of days until the strikers saw that they could not intimidate them into leaving and dispersed.

"Isn't there any other way to meet these troubles when they arise?"

"Not at present, and under similar circumstances. We have no proper legislation on the subject of trespass, and you can't very well go back to the common law proceeding on an information before a magistrate. Besides, with the influence of the Miner's Union against you, it is almost impossible to get testimony from witnesses who have full knowledge of facts. You have no idea of the class you have to deal with. There is not so much trouble with the Americans, Irish and negroes, but the English and Welsh contain a good many troublesome characters who work up most of the devilment. If I have received one anonymous letter

Threatening My Life,

I have had 20. The day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape, I was threatened by a mob, and at other times I have had to get out shooting irons in order to assert my right to stay where it was my plain duty to be. What is needed to put an end to this state of things, is legislation like that which stopped similar troubles in Pennsylvania. I know there will be some trouble in getting it, because there are always some members who will not act as they know they ought to act, for fear of losing a few votes, but the present Legislature is an exceptionally good one, and there have been, I think, enough exhibitions of the situation in our section to induce prompt and proper action by the two houses this winter.

Charlie Russell, whose industry helped to break up the Wheeling Standard, and who subsequently made considerable reputation as a historical novelist, lives here now, and he told me, yesterday, that he had a couple of brand new novels nearly ready for the press. WABASH, Ind., March 23.—Scarlet fever is epidemic in this city. One child has died. Three or four others were reported sick last evening, and nine new cases are announced this morning. All the city schools were closed at noon to-day and will remain so for two weeks.

The Kellogg case was first discussed, and it was determined if the Democrats developed strength enough to take it up that the Republicans would interpose obstacles to legislation and force an extra session rather than submit to the outrage of ousting Kellogg. cus was the appointment of an advisory committee, consisting of Messrs. Ferry, Windom, Dawes, Morrill, Logan, Allison, and Booth, to consider the funding bill with a view to securing harmonious Republican action on the same when it comes before the Senate.

Grant's Albany Reception.

ALBANY, N. Y., Jan. 17.—The reception of General Grant this afternoon was one of the greatest public demonstrations ever witnessed in this city. Fully 70,000 people were in the streets. Nearly all the buildings along the line of march were decorated with flags, &c., and the parade of the military was large and imposing. The Burgesses had the right of the line, followed by the Boys in Blue, then came the Governor's sleigh, in which were seated General Grant, Governor Cornell, and Adjutant-General Townsend, and following were the Tenth and Twenty-fifth Regiments. Reaching the executive mansion, the procession was drawn up in line, and the General, Governor, and Adjutant-General rode by, the military presenting arms. The General then entered the executive mansion. There was much enthusiasm manifested. Mrs. Grant was escorted to the executive mansion by Mrs. Cornell and her son in a sleigh immediately upon her arrival and before the procession started.

General Grant was serenaded to-night at the executive mansion by a club bearing his name, whom he addressed with brief thanks. After General Grant, Governor Cornell spoke. In the course of his remarks, Governor Cornell alluded to General Grant as one who, more than Washington, was first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.

The Whittaker Case.

New York, Jan. 17.—It is stated to-night arrangements for counsel in the Whittaker court-martial have been finally made. The report is that the defense will be conducted by Hon. James A. Whitney, of New York city, and also by ex-Governor D. H. Chamberlain, who was previously retained. Mr. Whitney is a life-long Democrat, and the fact that he will take a leading part in the management of the case is thought to forecast a temperate though vigorous defense on the actual merits of the matter with as little reference as possible to the color line. It is believed that an adjournment will need to be taken to enable the counsel to examine the immense mass of testimony—some 3,000 pages of manuscript in various handwriting—taken in the former case, and of which a copy is now available for the first time. This testimony cannot properly be used in the court-martial, but as it is the foundation of the charges, it is claimed to be only just that the defense should have time to become thoroughly acquainted with its contents.

A Virginia Tragedy.

RICHMOND, VA., Jan. 17.—A letter from Keysville, Charlotte County, Virginia, gives the particulars of a crime committed near that place on Sunday, in which Wilson Foulkes, a respectable clergyman, was the victim. It seems that Foulkes has, for some time past, been jealous of the attentions of Isaac Goulding, also colored, to his wife, and a few days since whipped her severely on account thereof, and told her that if the man came on his premisses again he would shoot her. On Sunday morning Goulding came again before Foulkes was up, and his wife, fearing he would carry out his threat of shooting her, crushed his skull with an axe while he was asleep, and then threw the body into a well to conceal the crime. Signs of blood being found between the house and the well, the woman was arrested and subsequently confessed that she had killed her husband. The murder created much excitement among the negroes in the neighborhood, and but for the counsels of the whites summary justice would have been visited upon the woman. She was committed to jail for trial.

MEHERRIN, VA., April 22—Lucinda Fowlkes (colored) was hanged at Lunenburg Courthouse to-day for the murder of her husband in January last. The execution was private, only the necessary officers and four others witnessed it.

[Second Dispatch.]

PARTICULARS OF THE HANGING.

MEHERRIN, VA., April 22.—Lucinda Fowlkes (colored) was hanged at Lunenburg Courthouse to-day for the murder of her husband in January last. The execution took place within an inclosure erected for the purpose in rear of the jail, the State law requiring all hangings to be done privately. Only the necessary officers, a preacher, and three other persons were present. An outside crowd of whites and negroes numbering 100 had gathered. There was no disorder. The condemned woman, on being visited this morning, was found quiet and apparently unconcerned. She said she had slept as usual during the night and had prayed a good deal. She had no dread of death, and trusted in a sin-giving God, to whom she was going. In answer to interrogatories she said that no one was implicated in the killing of her husband but herself. She had done it, and the negro Isaac Deans, who was suspected of complicity, was just as clear as an angel. Her husband was jealous of Deans, but without cause. She killed him because he was mean to her, constantly abusing and beating her. These statements she adhered to to the last. At about 10 o'clock a colored preacher was admitted to her cell, where he remained till the time of the execution. Quite a crowd, mostly colored, bad collected, and occasionally the voice of the preacher within could be heard giving out hymns, which were taken up and sung with religious fervor by those outside. At a few minutes after 11 the woman, dressed in a white cotton gown, was taken out by Sheriff J. W. Ellis and escorted by guards to the scaldold. But a few minutes were occupied in reading the death-sentence, tying her arms and lower limbs. She was asked if she desired to say anything, and answered. "No more than to bid all farewell." The black cap was then pulled over her face and the rope adjusted around her neck, and at a signal from the sheriff the hangman, who had been hired for the occasion, sprang the trap, and the murderess was swung into eternity at 11:35 o'clock. There was no struggle and but few muscular contractions. The pulse had ceased beating in eight minutes, and after hanging twelve minutes longer the body was taken down and placed in a rude coffin and buried near the jail. The body will doubtless be resurrected to-night, as the deceased had consented that the doctors should have it.

On the main road leading from Lunenburg county, Va., and distant from the village of Keysville, Charlotte county, two miles, was located the clearing and farm of Wilson Fowlkes, a colored man held in much esteem by the residents of both counties, most of whom knew him. Keysville was thrown into a flutter of excitement on the morning of January 15th last past by the intelligence that Fowlkes had been accidentally killed by falling into a well on his own premises. Fowlkes had hosts of friends in Keysville, where the people were accustomed to see him nearly every day, and consequently the crowd of both colors that determined to visit his place and ascertain for themselves the mode and manner of his death was numerous. They proceeded with the spirit of inquiry fully developed, and on the spot their searching investigation elicited the following facts:

The body of Fowlkes was found in the well; blood and brains (presumably his) were found on his bed and in various places in the room in which he slept, and also at intervals between the door of his house and the well in which his body was found. Brains were also found spattered on the inside of the well three feet from the top. The forehead of deceased was found completely crushed in as if by impact with some heavy blunt instrument wielded with irresistible force. Suspicion of the fate of Fowlkes was derived from the outgivings of his wife, who had suggested that he had fallen into the well. It appeared from further inquiry (all of which at a later stage of the proceeding assumed the shape of sworn testimony) that deceased and his wife had been heard quarrelling some days before the report of his death; that Mrs. Fowlkes was infatuated with a negro Lothario named Ike Deans; that her association with him went to the extreme of wifely depravity, and that her Dellah-like proclivities were exercised mostly in drawing Deans about the premises when its rightful lord and master was absent delving for a subsistence for his unfaithful partner and self and children. It was shown that he had frequently admonished his wife of the impropriety of her association with Deans, and that on the Sunday preceding his murder, not finding his monitions heeded, he had administered a severe castigation to the woman, which must have enraged her and led to the subsequent tragedy. Among the threats uttered by Fowlkes was one to the effect that if Deans was seen on the premises again he would shoot his wife. Deans did visit the wife early on Saturday morning, the day of the murder, and she, fearing doubtless that Fowlkes would awake, or perhaps carried away by guilty love for the destroyer of her matrimonial peace, resolved then and there to do away with her husband, and she proceeded to put the scheme into execution. She took the axe used about the premises, went to the room where her husband was asleep, and with one fearful blow crushed in his skull. She then took the body to the well and threw it in. The body was thrown into the well to create a false impression as to the cause of death. The murderess was an ignorant woman, did not seem to appreciate the enormity of the crime charged against her, and was alike indifferent to its results.

WOMAN HANGED.

LUNENBURG, Va., April 22.—Lucinda Fowlkes, the negro woman convicted of murdering her husband, was hung here to-day. The woman spent a restless night and got up early this morning. She had no appetite for the dainty breakfast her friends had sent her. At 11:40 she left her cell, accompanied by a negro preacher, and went to the scaffold, which was in the jail yard. Standing on the scaffold steps her drooping spirits seemed to revive, and she struck up the old-time negro melody, "Shout, my little sister; don't you grieve arter me," and it was taken up by the crowd of hundreds of negroes hanging around the jail walls, and sung in their peculiar Ethiopian way. The condemned woman appeared to find great relief in the singing of this and other hymns. She then bade farewell to her friends, telling several of them, "Tuko care of yourself; goodby," and then closed by saying, "Good-by all." She spoke kindly of her paramour, Isaac Dunn, and said several times that he knew nothing of her crime. Her hands and feet were then tied, the skirts of her dress bound about her feet, and the black cap drawn over her face. She trembled violently and had to be supported by the Sheriff and his assistants. At 11:52 the trap was sprung. She gave a few convulsive jerks, and after swinging eighteen minutes was pronounced dead.

THE CRIME.

On Saturday morning, Jan. 15 last, much excitement was created in Lunenburg County, Virginia, by the report that Wilson Fowlkes, a respectable colored man, had been accidentally killed by falling into a well on his promises. When the citizens of the county came to investigate the matter, however, they found that the man had been murdered. Before his body was flashed out of the well, blood-stains and portions of brain were found on the side of the well about three feet from the top; and this disproved the idea that Fowlkes had fallen in. It indicated that his dead body had been thrown in, and had grazed the side in going down. Clots of blood were also found in the yard leading from the house of the deceased to the well. Going into the house, it was seen that the blanket on the bed was covered with blood; and a cont belonging to the dead man was found hidden under the house, saturated with gore. Fowlkes was a married man, and lived with his wife, a grown daughter, and three younger children.

Suspicion was at once attached to his wife, Luolinda, and Issue Dean, a neighbor, with whom she was known to be too intimate. Fowlkes had frequently to leave his home to attend to his business, and would be absent from three to four days; and on these occasions Dean was in the habit of snoring around and spending his time with Fowlkes' wife. This scandalous intimacy at last reached the ears of the wronged husband, and he warned his wife to stop Dean from visiting her. Strange to say Fowlkes never appeared to lay any blame upon Dean, nor did he appear to cherish any animosity towards him. Dospite the warnings of her husband, the woman permitted Dean to visit her,—his visits being always timed when the husband was away.

ON THE SUNDAY BEFORE THE MURDER, Fowlkes, having learned of a recent visit of Dean, whipped his wife severely; and on Thursday he told her that, if Issue Dean over came there again, he would shoot her. From the determined way in which he spoke, the woman believed he would carry out his throat.

On Saturday morning, early, Dean came to Fowlkes' house while he was asleep. Luolinda, who was up at the time, saw him coming, and fearing that her husband might awake and catch him there, and kill her, at once determined to avort such an occurrence. Creoping stealthily into the room, and taking an ax with her, she stood over the bed, and with one blow
mined to invort such an occurrence. Creeping stoutly into the room, and taking an ax with her, she stood over the bed, and with one blow mashed in the skull of the sleeper. He turned over on his side with a spasmolio jerk, but no sound escaped his lips. The wife, however, in order to make sure of her work, dealt him another blow. She then came out and told Dean that her husband was inside, which announcement was sufficient to make him leave the place in quick time. The murderer then set to work to conceal her crime, and, lifting the bloody body of her husband upon her shoulders, curried it across the yard and

DROPPED IT INTO A WELL.

Going back into the house, she hid as well as possible all traces of her crime, and then woke up the rest of the family. She sent her grown daughter to the well to get some water, and told her that her father was there fixing the windlass. Her idea was to prepare the girl for the killing of the body and convey the impression that Powles had fallen in. She soon followed her daughter, and, pretending to be very much surprised at not seeing her husband there, suggested that he might have fallen into the well. Both then looked in, and the body was soon at the bottom. The neighbors, however, knew of the unlawful intercourse between Dean and the woman, and accused her of the crime. She then made a full confession, Dean was discharged. She was tried and sentenced to be hanged April 22. The Governor was asked to commute her sentence to imprisonment for life, but declined. The woman was very ignorant, and insisted that she was compelled to kill her husband in order to save her life. It is a very rare occurrence for a woman to be hung in the South. This is the first hanging of a female which has taken place in Virginia for twenty-five years.

WHOLESALE SHOOTING BY A LUNATIC.

CHICAGO, Sept. 2.—John C. Neal, a crazy stranger, last night about 1 o'clock, arose from bed in a lodging house at 353 Clark street, and suddenly placed a revolver to the head of another inmate of the room, David Fagin, and fired. He then darted down stairs to the office, and, with an Indian war whoop, shot the only occupant, an old Swede man named Springcard, in the back, then took a running jump out of the window and struck squarely on his feet and started down Clark street on a dead run, firing as he ran, and killing Henry Johnson, a negro, who attempted to stop him. Reaching Polk street, he fired at close range at Thomas Flynn, a railroad flagman, and William Wolf, the depot watchman, who were sitting together. Running still farther, he snapped his revolver twice at a policeman, who clubbed the excited lunatic, and after a violent struggle got him to the armory. CHICAGO, Sept. 2.—Fire broke out at 10 o'clock to night in the building on southeast corner of Lake and Franklin streets, No. 37 to 45, Franklin, which burned two houses before fully mastered. sandy-king-shakespeare-1881-11-08.A17:
"Sandy" King.
One of the cattle thieves recently executed by Judge Lynch at Shakspeare, was somewhat of a noted character, and had his life been prolonged, would, in all probability, have budded into a blooming desperado. It was he who, some months ago, stopped old man Heenan near Soldiers Holes, made him dismount from his horse, and as he started away with the animal the old man said, "It's pretty rough to leave an old man afoot like this." Upon which "Sandy" drew his pistol and with the remark, "You d—d old scoundrel, I'll give you something to remember me by," fired at him, the ball grazing his head.

His last exploit was at Lordsburg. He went into a store and ordered a bill of goods. When they were packed up the storekeeper said: "Who will I charge this to?" "To this!" replied "Sandy," placing his hand upon his pistol. "It's not good," said the clerk as he drew a pistol and shot him through the neck. But his neck was not to be broken by a bullet, and it got well just in time for the neck-tie matinee at which he played as end man.—Tombstone Nugget.

tom-johnson-clay-county-1881-02-18.A1:
Homicide in Clay.
Last Friday night there was a negro by the name of Tom Johnson killed by masked men near Joiner's store in Clay county. The circumstances as they reached in through reliable sources are about as follows: The negroes in that neighborhood, on the night of the killing had spotted of gathering and had dispersed to their homes. The deceased, Tom Johnson, a young negro man, had gone to the home of Jere Johnson, an old acquaintance and friend. While there, a body consisting of four masked men came on him and shot him so that the dead rose next day. A woman was also slightly shot. The next day, gone one of the negroes, backed up by the negroes of the community, proceeded to make an aidavit against the two young joines, ropes of Mr. Joe Joiner, and a couple of other young men whose names we have forgotten charging them with the crime. This amavit was sworn out before justice breached, and he and an invited associate were taking testimony the last we heard of it and we do not know the result of the trial, but it is fair to say nothing will come of it damaging to the young men implicated as they were prepared by witnesses and incontestible evidence to prove they were at home at the time the killing took place. The jury that held the inquest over the body returned a verdict in accordance with his view so far as the young men are concerned, that is to say their verdict was that he had come to his death in the hands of unknown parties. It was the opinion of Dr. Davis, our informant, that the affair was the result of a disposition among the negroes to correct certain abuses among themselves that was hard to reach by law.—Times.

A most atrocious crime was committed Saturday night at Kingston, a small hamlet in DeSoto parish, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield. Mr. Judd Scott, a young merchant doing business in Kingston left his boarding house about 9 o'clock p. m., going to his store where it was his custom to sleep. On Sunday morning his body was discovered lying about half way between Mrs. Beard's, where he boarded, and his store. The top of his head had been almost entirely blown off by a gun shot. The brains were scattered around, and hogs had partly devoured his body. His store and safe keys had been taken, and it was subsequently ascertained that the store and safe had been opened. No goods have been missed, and it is not known how much has been taken.

Mr Scott was one of the police jury-men in DeSoto parish, a man utterly without reproach and not known to have an enemy. the murder was evidently for the purpose of robbery.

Capt. Sample, sheriff of DeSoto parish, is on the ground and has arrested two negroes on strong circumstantial evidence. It is rumored this morning that an attempt was made last night to take the the prisoners from the sheriff for the purpose of lynching, but without success. Capt. Sample will protect the majesty of the law if posible, but it will be difficulty to restrain the people if the assassins are found. The citizens of DeSoto parish are determined to put down lawlessness.—Shreveport Standard.

The following letter received yesterday, gives some additional information concerning the murder, which has not been published until now:

MANSFIELD, July 19, 1881.

EDITOR TIMES.—Mr. M. J. Scott, a merchant and citizen of this parish, doing business at Kingston, was foully murdered on Saturday night, about 9 o'clock. He was at the time returning to the store from his boarding house, some two or three hundred yards distant with a lantern in his hand; was waylaid and shot in the back of the head, the shot entirely tearing away the back portion of the head, just as he was passing from the enclosure of his boarding-house. The news of this tragic event which reached us Sunday morning, was a great shock to the community. Mr. Scott was one of our best citizens and was not known to have an enemy in the world.

Sheriff Sample, with his usual energy and promptness, upon receipt of the first tidings, repaired to the scene of the tragedy and will probe the matter to the bottom, if it can be done. He sent to jail on Monday two negroes suspicioned of the crime. Last night the keys of the jail were forced from the jailor by some thirty or forty men presumed to reside in the vicinity of Kingston, and one of the prisoners, suspected, Wash Allen by name, was taken out, carried back to Kingston and hung there about daylight this morning. These men are generally known to be men of coolness and deliberation, and men who would not act hastily and without sufficient evidence. Allen is said to have confessed the crime before the hanging. The action of these gentlemen, so far as we have been able to learn, is approved in toto by the citizens of mansfield. It is idle to talk or think of the slow process of the law when so great a crime has been committed. Robbery was the incentive to the murder. All facts point to this conclusion. In this the murderer failed entirely. Very truly, JOSEPH JONES.

Minden Democrat: Saturday night as Mr. M. SAN ANTONIO, Tex., June 20.—The northbound stage of the San Antonio and Laredo line was stopped Saturday night near Rice station, on the line of the International & Great Northern Railway, about twenty-five miles from here, by one masked man, who compelled two passengers to alight and assist in riffling the mail sacks of checks, drafts, and Post-Officio money-order, amounting to $6,000. The stage was delayed two hours. The driver and passengers were not robbed of anything. It is thought the highwayman is the same one who robbed the stage between this city and Fredericksburg two weeks ago. John Williams, a negro under death sentence at Fort Concho for the murder of John Anderson last winter, broke fall last night and escaped. MURDER-DEATH OF THE MURDERER.
MARSHALL, Tex., June 20.—A tragedy occurred near here yesterday, resulting in the death of two men. Isaac Vergo and Robert Dlll had an altercation, which led to blows, and at length to a shooting affray, in which Vergo was killed by Dlll. The latter fled to the canebrakes, just over the Louisiana line, whilthor he was pursued by a Sheriff's posse. They at last overtook him in a brake, and called upon him to surrender. This he refused to do. The posse then opened fire upon the desperado. Twenty shots were fired, resulting in the instant death of Dlll, whose body was literally riddled with rille-balls.

MURDER ON A HIGHWAY.

St. Joseph, Mo., June 20.—Chris Callahan and John Lening met on the road a short distance from De Kalk, Mo., Saturday night, and got into a quarrel. Callahan jumped from his wagon, advanced on Lening with a revolver in one hand and a knife in the other, and threatened to kill him. Lening drew a revolver and fired; the ball striking Callahan in the abdomen, inflicting a wound from which he died yesterday. Lening, who is an old man, gave himself up, and was let out on bail of $1,000. Callahan was a young man only recently married.

An attempt to arrest him was made, but, though dangerously wounded by Marshal Hall, he escaped to the woods and is still at large. A number of persons are pursuing him.

Boston, June 20.—Several additional attachments upon the property of the Globe Company were served to-day. The 85,000 which Derney deposited with the Clerk of the Court, in lieu of ball, were attached by two persons. Attachments were also placed upon the funds standing in the name of the Company with F. Dernorr, Mich., June 20.—Constable William Close was arrested here this morning, and will be tried on several charges of blackmailing preferred by country and suburban saloonkeepers, who allege that he has made them pay roundly for the privilege of selling liquor on Sundays, etc., without being complained against.

KILLED HIS FATHER-IN-LAW.

SEXATONIA, Miss., June 20.—John A. Day, City Marshal of Strayhorn, a village twelve miles west of Senptobia, had his throat cut from ear to ear last Saturday by his son-in-law, a young man named Mayfield. The murderer escaped. The difficulty originated over the ownership of a saddle.

GRANT'S JEWELS.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Sr. Louis, June 20.—The cases of Elsie King and John L. Fitzpatrick, who were arrested and charged with stealing the Grant jewels, were called in the Court of Criminal Correction for preliminary examination, but, as Gen. Grant's attendance could not be secured, the cases were continued.

BLOWING UP AN ENEMY.

Shasta, Cal., June 20.—The store of Dr. Conkling at Centreville was blown up by giant powder at 2 a.m. The building, stock, and outhouses were totally wrecked. Conkling, who slept in the building, was taken from the ruins in a critical condition. It is supposed to be the work of an enemy.

SHOT FIVE TIMES.

Memphis, Tenn., June 20.—This morning, near Looxahoma, Miss., a young man named Taylor D. Ward shot and mortally wounded William Rogers. No particulars as to the cause of the shooting have been received. Rogers was shot five times, and will die.

CHARLESTON, Ind., June 20.—Mrs. Mary McCoy was robbed of $1,000 last evening, by a thief who entered the house while the family were at supper in the rear of the house. No clew.
